old: “When you get home, you’ll take revenge
new: “‘When you get home, you’ll take revenge
reason: Butler opens this paragraph “‘When you get home — Teiresias is still speaking (his prophecy begins at ¶7 with “‘You want to know) — and the candidate drops the nested single quote, so the prophecy reads as Odysseus's own frame narration (D4; PUNCTUATION §5 'a wrong opening mark is a wrong speaker'); the drafter's note that the source has no mark here is incorrect.

old: All that I’ve said will come true.
new: All that I’ve said will come true.’
reason: Butler closes the prophecy 'All that I have said will come true].’' with a single closing quote (the class-C bracket mark is dropped per D12, the quotation mark is not); without it the nested speech never closes and ¶9's ‘This must be… opens inside an unclosed quotation.

old: and your people will be blessed
new: and your people will bless you
reason: Butler: 'and your people shall bless you' — the people are the actors and Odysseus the one blessed; the candidate reverses this into a passive about the people's own blessedness, a changed statement in the prophecy.

old: maidens who had died for love
new: maidens who had been crossed in love
reason: Butler: 'maids who had been crossed in love' (thwarted/disappointed in love); 'died for love' invents a cause of death Butler does not state.

old: Castor the horse-tamer and Pollux the mighty boxer
new: Castor the horse-tamer and Polydeuces the mighty boxer
reason: Butler's 'Pollux' is the Latin form of Polydeuces; widened D5 (ledger, 2026-09-13: 'any figure Butler names in a ROMAN form takes the Greek one', which names 'Castor and Pollux (Polydeuces)' among the cases Book 11 will meet) and ODY-RULES ('Hercules→Heracles and other Roman forms of figures per D5') apply exactly as they did to Bacchus→Dionysus in ¶25 — coordinator to confirm.

old: At that spot you must plant the oar
new: At this you must plant the oar
reason: Butler's sentential 'on this you must fix the oar' is a time connective (thereupon), not a place; GLOSSARY's Book 4 row fixes sentential 'On this' → 'At this', which accepted B10-P044 applies to the same instructional future ('At this, many dead men’s ghosts will come').

old: With that, Tiresias’s ghost returned
new: At this, Tiresias’s ghost returned
reason: Butler: 'On this the ghost of Teiresias went back'; GLOSSARY (Book 4 row) fixes sentential 'On this' → 'At this', held in accepted Books 9 and 10 (B09-P038, B09-P040, B10-P002, B10-P015, B10-P036) and applied by this candidate itself at ¶53's second instance.

old: With that, Heracles went back down
new: At this, Heracles went back down
reason: Butler: 'On this Hercules went down again'; same fixed 'On this' → 'At this' row, and the same paragraph's second 'On this I hastened' is already rendered 'At this I hurried'.

old: how we fell in that hall, with the wine bowl
new: how we fell in that gallery, with the mixing-bowl
reason: Butler: 'the way in which we fell in that cloister, with the mixing bowl'; GLOSSARY fixes 'cloister' → 'gallery' (applied at ¶27 of this Book) and accepted Books 1, 3 and 4 print 'mixing-bowl' (D15); 'hall' and 'wine bowl' are third renderings (D29).

old: for a wedding feast, banquet, or celebration of some great lord
new: for the wedding breakfast, or shared feast, or gorgeous banquet of some great lord
reason: Butler: 'for the wedding breakfast, or picnic, or gorgeous banquet of some great nobleman'; the candidate drops 'gorgeous' and reorders the three meals so the great lord's banquet is no longer the climax.

old: I might have made him speak despite his anger, or I might have continued
new: I would have made him speak despite his anger, or I would have gone on
reason: Butler: 'I should have made him talk to me… or I should have gone on talking' — conditional certainty (would have), not possibility; 'might' adds a hedge.

old: I would have seen still others who are gone—Theseus
new: I would have seen still others who are gone before, whom I longed to see—Theseus
reason: Butler: 'still other of them that are gone before, whom I would fain have seen—Theseus and Pirithous'; the clause of Odysseus's desire is dropped.

old: I felt terrible sorrow when I saw him and cried out, ‘Elpenor, how
new: I was very sorry for him and wept when I saw him. ‘Elpenor,’ I said, ‘how
reason: Butler: 'I was very sorry for him, and cried when I saw him: ‘Elpenor,’ said I' — 'cried' is weeping (the speech is introduced separately by 'said I'); 'cried out' loses the tears and 'terrible sorrow' intensifies 'very sorry'.

old: a strange, unearthly wailing
new: a strange kind of screaming
reason: Butler: 'a strange kind of screaming sound'; 'wailing' softens the screaming and 'unearthly' is added.

old: Clytemnestra plotted against you during your absence
new: Clytemnestra plotted against you too during your absence
reason: Butler: 'Clytemnestra hatched mischief against you too' — 'too' carries the point that the house's women ruined the Atreidae twice (Helen, then Clytemnestra).

old: he received his fair share of the prize money
new: he received his handsome share of the prize money
reason: Butler: 'he got his handsome share of the prize money' — generous, not merely equitable; 'fair' shifts the sense.

old: and carry it until you reach
new: and carry it on and on until you reach
reason: Butler: 'carry it on and on, till you come to a country' — the repetition conveys the length of the journey.

old: having slept in Zeus’s arms
new: having slept in the arms of Zeus himself
reason: Butler: 'who could boast of having slept in the arms of even Jove himself' — the emphasis of her boast is dropped.

old: you’ll have fine twin sons
new: you’ll have fine twins
reason: Butler: 'you will have fine twins'; 'sons' anticipates ¶18 in the god's mouth.

old: whom Theseus was carrying from Crete to Athens
new: whom Theseus was carrying off from Crete to Athens
reason: Butler: 'whom Theseus was carrying off from Crete' — 'off' marks the abduction/elopement; bare 'carrying' flattens it.

old: leaving behind avenging spirits to torment him for his outraged mother
new: and the avenging spirits haunted him for his outraged mother
reason: Butler: 'and the avenging spirits haunted him as for an outraged mother' — no agency is given to Epicaste; 'leaving behind' makes her the one who sets them on him.

old: The evenings are still long
new: The evenings are still at their longest
reason: Butler: 'The evenings are still at their longest' — Alcinous's point is that the night has plenty left.

old: Then spoke aged hero Echeneus
new: Then the aged hero Echeneus spoke
reason: Butler: 'Then spoke the aged hero Echeneus'; dropping the article leaves a headline-style phrase that stumbles aloud.

old: where lies the land and city of the Cimmerians
new: where the land and city of the Cimmerians lie
reason: Inverted 'where lies the land' is archaic word order; a listener parses it more slowly than plain subject-verb order. Minor, not blocking.

old: Now I beg you by everyone you left behind—though they’re not here—by your wife, by the father who raised you as a child, and by Telemachus, who is your house’s only hope, do what I’m about to ask.
new: So I beg you, in the name of everyone you left behind—though they’re not here—your wife, the father who raised you as a child, and Telemachus, who is your house’s only hope: please do what I’m about to ask.
reason: Four 'by X' oath clauses pile up before the actual request ('do what I'm about to ask') finally lands, so a listener has to hold the sentence's purpose in suspension for a long stretch. Front-loading 'I beg you' and closing with a clear colon before the request would let the ear track it more easily.

old: nor do they know anything about ships and oars that serve as a ship’s wings
new: nor do they know anything about ships, or about oars, which serve as a ship’s wings
reason: 'ships and oars that serve as a ship's wings' reads as if the relative clause could modify 'ships and oars' together; a comma/rephrase makes clear it's only the oars being likened to wings.

old: He has to host many guests, as he must, considering his position as a magistrate and how everyone invites him.
new: He has to entertain a great deal, as of course he must, given his position as a magistrate, and everyone invites him out as well.
reason: As written the sentence is self-contradictory to a listener: it says Telemachus 'hosts' guests, then gives the reason as 'how everyone invites him' — which sounds like he is the one being invited out, not the one doing the hosting. The logic doesn't resolve on a single hearing. 'Magistrate' is also an anachronistic, legalistic-sounding term that doesn't fit a young prince keeping open house. [lead: wording adjusted to keep Butler’s terms]

old: I heard Priam’s daughter Cassandra scream as Clytemnestra killed her beside me.
new: I heard Priam’s daughter Cassandra scream as my wife, Clytemnestra, killed her beside me.
reason: Agamemnon has only just referred to her as 'my wicked wife'; this is the first time the name 'Clytemnestra' appears in the book, with nothing tying the name back to 'my wife.' A listener has no way to know at this moment who Clytemnestra is.

old: The fleet descendant of Aeacus recognized me and spoke mournfully
new: Achilles, the fleet descendant of Aeacus, recognized me and spoke mournfully
reason: Achilles was just named one sentence earlier, then immediately referred to only by an unglossed patronymic epithet ('descendant of Aeacus'); a listener has to work backward to confirm this is still Achilles. Re-anchoring the name removes the stumble.

old: Many other Ceteians fell around Eurypylus because of a woman’s bribes.
new: Many other Ceteians fell around him because a woman took bribes—his mother, bribed with gifts to send him to the war.
reason: 'because of a woman's bribes' names no one and explains nothing; a first-time listener has no way to attach meaning to 'a woman' or 'bribes' here, and the sentence just moves on. It needs the minimal context of who bribed whom and why. [lead: wording adjusted to keep Butler’s terms]

old: Moreover, when all the bravest of the Argives went inside the horse Epeus had built, and it fell to me to decide when we should open our ambush or stay hidden, though all the other leaders and chief men among the Danaans were wiping their eyes and trembling in every limb, I never once saw him turn pale or brush a tear from his cheek.
new: Moreover, when all the bravest of the Argives climbed inside the horse Epeus had built, it fell to me to decide when we should spring our ambush or stay hidden. All the other leaders and chief men among the Danaans were wiping their eyes and trembling in every limb, but I never once saw him turn pale or brush a tear from his cheek.
reason: One sentence stacks a 'when' clause, an embedded decision, and a 'though' concession before reaching its main point; splitting it into two sentences lets each idea land on its own breath.
